“He was home with me all the time, and that's when I
noticed some eye fluttering. At first, I just thought that he
was tired and ready to fall asleep,” she says. “But about a
month into it, I knew something wasn’t right.”

His pediatrician requested overnight monitoring of Kai's
brain to determine whether it was experiencing seizure
activity. But just five minutes into the monitoring, they
detected significant seizure activity, Jessica says. Kai was
soon diagnosed with epilepsy, a disorder in which nerve
cell activity in the brain is disturbed, causing seizures.

"It was kind of scary because other than one family

plain_text:
Kai's doctors quickly started him on anti-seizure
medication. Meanwhile, they ordered genetic testing
and imaging of his brain to better pinpoint why he was
having seizures. The results of the imaging showed
normal brain development. Genetic testing, however,
revealed SYNGAP1—a rare gene mutation discovered
in 2009. SYNGAP1 causes developmental delays and
recurrent seizures.

Kai is now 3 years old, and Jessica says treating his
epilepsy with medication has been difficult. Finding the
correct combination and dosages takes time. Kai currently
takes four anti-seizure medications. They have reduced
his seizures from up to 10 an hour to about five an hour.

mind every day."
